PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38!
www.YESon38.com
CON
California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.

8. Endorsement: Vote ‘yes’ on these California state propositions
https://www.dailycal.org/opinion/editorials/endorsement-vote-yes-on-these-california-state-propositions/article_5567c2e3-ef3b-42ae-b2c7-85aabfdcc1c3.html
### Proposition 38: NO
Proposition 38 would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to fund research into treatments for cancer, Alzheimer’s and other diseases that can be fought through immunotherapy.
It would also require the drugs developed through this research to be sold at discounted rates.
At face value, this proposition seems reasonable.
However, a deeper look into Prop.
38 shows us that it is rife with issues.
CalMatters found that about 50% of the funding sourced from Prop.
38 is likely to go to the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy — a nonprofit that had three employees as of last month.
It is unclear whether this institute has the capacity to handle billions of dollars.
Further, the writer of the proposition, Gary K. Michelson, is the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy’s primary funder.
While we acknowledge the pressing need for more medical research funding, the glaring problems with Prop.
38 make us hesitant to endorse it.
Vote “no” on Prop.
38.

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38!
www.YESon38.com
CON
California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38!
www.YESon38.com
CON
California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
FOR
YES on 38: Californians for
Life-Saving Immunology
Research and Cures

### Proposition 38: NO
Proposition 38 would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to fund research into treatments for cancer, Alzheimer’s and other diseases that can be fought through immunotherapy.
It would also require the drugs developed through this research to be sold at discounted rates.
At face value, this proposition seems reasonable.
However, a deeper look into Prop.
38 shows us that it is rife with issues.
CalMatters found that about 50% of the funding sourced from Prop.
38 is likely to go to the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy — a nonprofit that had three employees as of last month.
It is unclear whether this institute has the capacity to handle billions of dollars.
Further, the writer of the proposition, Gary K. Michelson, is the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy’s primary funder.
While we acknowledge the pressing need for more medical research funding, the glaring problems with Prop.
38 make us hesitant to endorse it.
Vote “no” on Prop.
38.

California’s Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research and send half to one UCLA-affiliated institute
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research. The measure's seven criteria for the institute that receives half the money match the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder has given the campaign at least $50 million. Here is the full picture.
by
Dr. Jennifer Trimpey | Specialist (https://californiatoday.com/author/jennifer-trimpey/)

Proposition 38 would let California borrow $8.4 billion to pay for research in immunology and immunotherapy, the science of using the body's immune system to prevent and treat disease. Half of the money would go to a single nonprofit research institute chosen by the state Department of Public Health under seven criteria written into the measure. The other half would be awarded as competitive grants by a council of university representatives. At least $2.1 billion of each half must be spent on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year from the General Fund for about 20 years.
Prop 38, the "California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the most one-sided money race among them: $76.2 million in top-donor support against an opposition committee that has reported $3,782. It led 55% to 42% in PPIC's September survey, the only public poll to test it. Governor Gavin Newsom and both major parties support it; every newspaper editorial board we could read opposes it.

This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a new division to the Health and Safety Code authorizing $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, the kind the state repays from the General Fund with interest. After bond costs and a cap of 2% for state administration, the proceeds are split two ways:
50% to "a single nonprofit medical research institute" selected by the Department of Public Health "for the purpose of conducting or directing health science research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy." The department must sign a funding agreement with the institute within 90 days of the measure taking effect and review it every five years. The measure also appropriates $100 million from the General Fund as a start-up loan to the institute, to be repaid from bond proceeds.
50% to competitive grants for public and nonprofit universities and nonprofit research institutions, awarded "as individualized grants for specific research projects through an application process," not as block grants. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council decides who gets them. Its seven-member executive committee is appointed by the chancellors of UC Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco, and that committee appoints 10 to 15 more members from other California nonprofit universities and research institutions, for a council of 17 to 22. UCLA's appointee serves as the council's first chair.
Each half carries a floor: "not less than" $2.1 billion must be spent on "the prevention, treatment, and cure of cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease." Grants are limited to researchers and projects "primarily located within this state," indirect costs are capped at 20% of a grant, and no money may go to for-profit companies. Every grant recipient must offer the selected institute "the opportunity to substantially participate in and collaborate on the funded research," and must offer UCLA the same opportunity on any clinical trials.
Proposition 38's $8.4 billion is splitting evenly between one nonprofit research institute and a council-run grant program, with $2.1 billion of each half reserved for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. The measure can be amended only by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature, and never on "the allocation and disbursement of bond proceeds or the purposes for which bond proceeds may be expended."

**The basics**
The Trump administration has frozen, terminated or delayed billions in congressionally approved research grants since last year.
Proposition 38 aims to backfill some of that loss by creating a stable source of money to fund immunology and immunotherapy research.
Proposition 38 would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research to uncover treatments that help the immune system fight diseases such as cancer or Alzheimer’s disease more efficiently.

The measure would require at least $4.2 billion of the funds to be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s.
It also would authorize the state to enter a partnership with an immunology and immunotherapy research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health and allocate half of the bond revenue to it.
The remaining funds would be used for competitive grants that focus solely on immunology and immunotherapy research.
Californians would take on an increased cost of $500 million to $600 million annually to repay the bond for about 20 years, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.

## Proposition 38
**The basics**
The Trump administration has frozen, terminated or delayed billions in congressionally approved research grants since last year.
Proposition 38 aims to backfill some of that loss by creating a stable source of money to fund immunology and immunotherapy research.
Proposition 38 would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research to uncover treatments that help the immune system fight diseases such as cancer or Alzheimer’s disease more efficiently.

The measure would require at least $4.2 billion of the funds to be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s.
It also would authorize the state to enter a partnership with an immunology and immunotherapy research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health and allocate half of the bond revenue to it.
The remaining funds would be used for competitive grants that focus solely on immunology and immunotherapy research.
Californians would take on an increased cost of $500 million to $600 million annually to repay the bond for about 20 years, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.

How this is built
Proposition 38 is forecast as a bonds and budgets measure whose Yes vote leans to neither party . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). California’s Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research and send half to one UCLA-affiliated institute
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research. The measure's seven criteria for the institute that receives half the money match the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder has given the campaign at least $50 million. Here is the full picture.
by
Dr. Jennifer Trimpey | Specialist (https://californiatoday.com/author/jennifer-trimpey/)
Updated
October 16, 2026

Proposition 38 would let California borrow $8.4 billion to pay for research in immunology and immunotherapy, the science of using the body's immune system to prevent and treat disease. Half of the money would go to a single nonprofit research institute chosen by the state Department of Public Health under seven criteria written into the measure. The other half would be awarded as competitive grants by a council of university representatives. At least $2.1 billion of each half must be spent on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year from the General Fund for about 20 years.
Prop 38, the "California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the most one-sided money race among them: $76.2 million in top-donor support against an opposition committee that has reported $3,782. It led 55% to 42% in PPIC's September survey, the only public poll to test it. Governor Gavin Newsom and both major parties support it; every newspaper editorial board we could read opposes it.

Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion and split it between one institute and a grant council:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a new division to the Health and Safety Code authorizing $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, the kind the state repays from the General Fund with interest. After bond costs and a cap of 2% for state administration, the proceeds are split two ways:
50% to "a single nonprofit medical research institute" selected by the Department of Public Health "for the purpose of conducting or directing health science research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy." The department must sign a funding agreement with the institute within 90 days of the measure taking effect and review it every five years. The measure also appropriates $100 million from the General Fund as a start-up loan to the institute, to be repaid from bond proceeds.
50% to competitive grants for public and nonprofit universities and nonprofit research institutions, awarded "as individualized grants for specific research projects through an application process," not as block grants. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council decides who gets them. Its seven-member executive committee is appointed by the chancellors of UC Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco, and that committee appoints 10 to 15 more members from other California nonprofit universities and research institutions, for a council of 17 to 22. UCLA's appointee serves as the council's first chair.
Each half carries a floor: "not less than" $2.1 billion must be spent on "the prevention, treatment, and cure of cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease." Grants are limited to researchers and projects "primarily located within this state," indirect costs are capped at 20% of a grant, and no money may go to for-profit companies. Every grant recipient must offer the selected institute "the opportunity to substantially participate in and collaborate on the funded research," and must offer UCLA the same opportunity on any clinical trials.
Proposition 38's $8.4 billion is splitting evenly between one nonprofit research institute and a council-run grant program, with $2.1 billion of each half reserved for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. The measure can be amended only by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature, and never on "the allocation and disbursement of bond proceeds or the purposes for which bond proceeds may be expended."

California’s Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research and send half to one UCLA-affiliated institute
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research. The measure's seven criteria for the institute that receives half the money match the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder has given the campaign at least $50 million. Here is the full picture.
by
Dr. Jennifer Trimpey | Specialist (https://californiatoday.com/author/jennifer-trimpey/)
Updated
October 16, 2026
Link copied!
Copy failed!
Proposition 38 would let California borrow $8.4 billion to pay for research in immunology and immunotherapy, the science of using the body's immune system to prevent and treat disease. Half of the money would go to a single nonprofit research institute chosen by the state Department of Public Health under seven criteria written into the measure. The other half would be awarded as competitive grants by a council of university representatives. At least $2.1 billion of each half must be spent on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year from the General Fund for about 20 years.
Prop 38, the "California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the most one-sided money race among them: $76.2 million in top-donor support against an opposition committee that has reported $3,782. It led 55% to 42% in PPIC's September survey, the only public poll to test it. Governor Gavin Newsom and both major parties support it; every newspaper editorial board we could read opposes it.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) This guide covers what the text does, the three research bonds California has already approved or scheduled, the organization the institute criteria describe, the measure's transparency rules, the royalty and discount provisions, the cost, the money behind each side, the arguments and the polling.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion and split it between one institute and a grant council:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a new division to the Health and Safety Code authorizing $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, the kind the state repays from the General Fund with interest. After bond costs and a cap of 2% for state administration, the proceeds are split two ways:
50% to "a single nonprofit medical research institute" selected by the Department of Public Health "for the purpose of conducting or directing health science research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy." The department must sign a funding agreement with the institute within 90 days of the measure taking effect and review it every five years. The measure also appropriates $100 million from the General Fund as a start-up loan to the institute, to be repaid from bond proceeds.
50% to competitive grants for public and nonprofit universities and nonprofit research institutions, awarded "as individualized grants for specific research projects through an application process," not as block grants. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council decides who gets them. Its seven-member executive committee is appointed by the chancellors of UC Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco, and that committee appoints 10 to 15 more members from other California nonprofit universities and research institutions, for a council of 17 to 22. UCLA's appointee serves as the council's first chair.
Each half carries a floor: "not less than" $2.1 billion must be spent on "the prevention, treatment, and cure of cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease." Grants are limited to researchers and projects "primarily located within this state," indirect costs are capped at 20% of a grant, and no money may go to for-profit companies. Every grant recipient must offer the selected institute "the opportunity to substantially participate in and collaborate on the funded research," and must offer UCLA the same opportunity on any clinical trials.
Proposition 38's $8.4 billion is splitting evenly between one nonprofit research institute and a council-run grant program, with $2.1 billion of each half reserved for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. The measure can be amended only by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature, and never on "the allocation and disbursement of bond proceeds or the purposes for which bond proceeds may be expended."
California has borrowed for medical research twice before and has a third research bond scheduled for 2028:

## Proposition 38
**The basics**
The Trump administration has frozen, terminated or delayed billions in congressionally approved research grants since last year.
Proposition 38 aims to backfill some of that loss by creating a stable source of money to fund immunology and immunotherapy research.
Proposition 38 would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research to uncover treatments that help the immune system fight diseases such as cancer or Alzheimer’s disease more efficiently.

The measure would require at least $4.2 billion of the funds to be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s.
It also would authorize the state to enter a partnership with an immunology and immunotherapy research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health and allocate half of the bond revenue to it.
The remaining funds would be used for competitive grants that focus solely on immunology and immunotherapy research.
Californians would take on an increased cost of $500 million to $600 million annually to repay the bond for about 20 years, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.

California’s Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research and send half to one UCLA-affiliated institute
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research. The measure's seven criteria for the institute that receives half the money match the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder has given the campaign at least $50 million. Here is the full picture.
by
Dr. Jennifer Trimpey | Specialist (https://californiatoday.com/author/jennifer-trimpey/)
Updated
October 16, 2026

Proposition 38 would let California borrow $8.4 billion to pay for research in immunology and immunotherapy, the science of using the body's immune system to prevent and treat disease. Half of the money would go to a single nonprofit research institute chosen by the state Department of Public Health under seven criteria written into the measure. The other half would be awarded as competitive grants by a council of university representatives. At least $2.1 billion of each half must be spent on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year from the General Fund for about 20 years.
Prop 38, the "California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the most one-sided money race among them: $76.2 million in top-donor support against an opposition committee that has reported $3,782. It led 55% to 42% in PPIC's September survey, the only public poll to test it. Governor Gavin Newsom and both major parties support it; every newspaper editorial board we could read opposes it.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) This guide covers what the text does, the three research bonds California has already approved or scheduled, the organization the institute criteria describe, the measure's transparency rules, the royalty and discount provisions, the cost, the money behind each side, the arguments and the polling.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion and split it between one institute and a grant council:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a new division to the Health and Safety Code authorizing $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, the kind the state repays from the General Fund with interest. After bond costs and a cap of 2% for state administration, the proceeds are split two ways:
50% to "a single nonprofit medical research institute" selected by the Department of Public Health "for the purpose of conducting or directing health science research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy." The department must sign a funding agreement with the institute within 90 days of the measure taking effect and review it every five years. The measure also appropriates $100 million from the General Fund as a start-up loan to the institute, to be repaid from bond proceeds.
50% to competitive grants for public and nonprofit universities and nonprofit research institutions, awarded "as individualized grants for specific research projects through an application process," not as block grants. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council decides who gets them. Its seven-member executive committee is appointed by the chancellors of UC Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco, and that committee appoints 10 to 15 more members from other California nonprofit universities and research institutions, for a council of 17 to 22. UCLA's appointee serves as the council's first chair.
Each half carries a floor: "not less than" $2.1 billion must be spent on "the prevention, treatment, and cure of cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease." Grants are limited to researchers and projects "primarily located within this state," indirect costs are capped at 20% of a grant, and no money may go to for-profit companies. Every grant recipient must offer the selected institute "the opportunity to substantially participate in and collaborate on the funded research," and must offer UCLA the same opportunity on any clinical trials.
Proposition 38's $8.4 billion is splitting evenly between one nonprofit research institute and a council-run grant program, with $2.1 billion of each half reserved for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. The measure can be amended only by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature, and never on "the allocation and disbursement of bond proceeds or the purposes for which bond proceeds may be expended."
California has borrowed for medical research twice before and has a third research bond scheduled for 2028:

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38!
www.YESon38.com
CON
California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.

### Proposition 38: NO
Proposition 38 would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to fund research into treatments for cancer, Alzheimer’s and other diseases that can be fought through immunotherapy.
It would also require the drugs developed through this research to be sold at discounted rates.
At face value, this proposition seems reasonable.
However, a deeper look into Prop.
38 shows us that it is rife with issues.
CalMatters found that about 50% of the funding sourced from Prop.
38 is likely to go to the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy — a nonprofit that had three employees as of last month.
It is unclear whether this institute has the capacity to handle billions of dollars.
Further, the writer of the proposition, Gary K. Michelson, is the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy’s primary funder.
While we acknowledge the pressing need for more medical research funding, the glaring problems with Prop.
38 make us hesitant to endorse it.
Vote “no” on Prop.
38.

## Proposition 38
**The basics**
The Trump administration has frozen, terminated or delayed billions in congressionally approved research grants since last year.
Proposition 38 aims to backfill some of that loss by creating a stable source of money to fund immunology and immunotherapy research.
Proposition 38 would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research to uncover treatments that help the immune system fight diseases such as cancer or Alzheimer’s disease more efficiently.
...
Oct. 26, 2026
...
The measure would require at least $4.2 billion of the funds to be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s.
It also would authorize the state to enter a partnership with an immunology and immunotherapy research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health and allocate half of the bond revenue to it.
The remaining funds would be used for competitive grants that focus solely on immunology and immunotherapy research.
Californians would take on an increased cost of $500 million to $600 million annually to repay the bond for about 20 years, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.

How this is built
Proposition 38 is forecast as a bonds and budgets measure whose Yes vote leans to neither party . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). California’s Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research and send half to one UCLA-affiliated institute
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research. The measure's seven criteria for the institute that receives half the money match the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder has given the campaign at least $50 million. Here is the full picture.
by
Dr. Jennifer Trimpey | Specialist (https://californiatoday.com/author/jennifer-trimpey/)
Updated
October 16, 2026

Proposition 38 would let California borrow $8.4 billion to pay for research in immunology and immunotherapy, the science of using the body's immune system to prevent and treat disease. Half of the money would go to a single nonprofit research institute chosen by the state Department of Public Health under seven criteria written into the measure. The other half would be awarded as competitive grants by a council of university representatives. At least $2.1 billion of each half must be spent on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year from the General Fund for about 20 years.
Prop 38, the "California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the most one-sided money race among them: $76.2 million in top-donor support against an opposition committee that has reported $3,782. It led 55% to 42% in PPIC's September survey, the only public poll to test it. Governor Gavin Newsom and both major parties support it; every newspaper editorial board we could read opposes it.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) This guide covers what the text does, the three research bonds California has already approved or scheduled, the organization the institute criteria describe, the measure's transparency rules, the royalty and discount provisions, the cost, the money behind each side, the arguments and the polling.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion and split it between one institute and a grant council:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a new division to the Health and Safety Code authorizing $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, the kind the state repays from the General Fund with interest. After bond costs and a cap of 2% for state administration, the proceeds are split two ways:
50% to "a single nonprofit medical research institute" selected by the Department of Public Health "for the purpose of conducting or directing health science research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy." The department must sign a funding agreement with the institute within 90 days of the measure taking effect and review it every five years. The measure also appropriates $100 million from the General Fund as a start-up loan to the institute, to be repaid from bond proceeds.
50% to competitive grants for public and nonprofit universities and nonprofit research institutions, awarded "as individualized grants for specific research projects through an application process," not as block grants. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council decides who gets them. Its seven-member executive committee is appointed by the chancellors of UC Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco, and that committee appoints 10 to 15 more members from other California nonprofit universities and research institutions, for a council of 17 to 22. UCLA's appointee serves as the council's first chair.
Each half carries a floor: "not less than" $2.1 billion must be spent on "the prevention, treatment, and cure of cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease." Grants are limited to researchers and projects "primarily located within this state," indirect costs are capped at 20% of a grant, and no money may go to for-profit companies. Every grant recipient must offer the selected institute "the opportunity to substantially participate in and collaborate on the funded research," and must offer UCLA the same opportunity on any clinical trials.
Proposition 38's $8.4 billion is splitting evenly between one nonprofit research institute and a council-run grant program, with $2.1 billion of each half reserved for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. The measure can be amended only by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature, and never on "the allocation and disbursement of bond proceeds or the purposes for which bond proceeds may be expended."
California has borrowed for medical research twice before and has a third research bond scheduled for 2028:
